This study compared absolute spectral power and coherence features for classifying OCD patients and healthy controls using a SHAP-interpretable Random Forest framework. Resting-state EEG data from 46 OCD patients and 95 healthy controls were analyzed, with the control group balanced to 46 participants. Separate Random Forest models were trained for absolute power and coherence features using a leakage-free 5-fold cross-validation pipeline in which SHAP-based feature selection was performed exclusively within each training fold. The absolute-power model performed at chance level, whereas the coherence model showed modest classification performance. However, no feature was consistently selected across all folds, indicating substantial instability in the identified predictors. These findings suggest that coherence may contain more discriminative information than absolute power in this dataset, but neither feature class provided clinically reliable classification. More broadly, the results caution against overinterpreting high accuracies reported in small EEG-ML datasets without leakage-free validation, feature-stability analysis, and external replication.

articles.title: Pupil Dynamics Are Associated with Individual Differences in Visual Time-Reproduction Accuracy
articles.authors: Amir Jahanian Najafabadi; Khaled Bagh; Kayser Christoph
articles.abstract: Accurate temporal reproduction depends on the interaction between sensory encoding, attention, motor production, and bodily state. Visual timing is especially likely to be influenced by oculomotor behavior because the eyes continuously stabilize, interrupt, and resample visual input through pupil-linked arousal changes. The present study tested whether spontaneous pupil fluctuations track moment-to-moment timing or stable individual differences. Eighty healthy adults reproduced visually presented intervals at a fixed viewing distance of 120 cm while pupil size was recorded continuously at 500 Hz. After preprocessing, 4,104 valid participant-trials were available. The primary outcomes were signed relative reproduction error, indexing directional bias, and absolute error, indexing timing precision. Mixed-effects models and participant-level regressions were used to examine within-participant and between-participant associations. Pupil metrics showed weaker trial-level effects, but reduced participant-level pupil models predicted both signed bias and absolute error, suggesting that stable pupil-linked arousal profiles relate to individual timing precision. These findings suggest that the eyes do not merely record visual time-varying events; their stabilization, interruption, and arousal-linked dynamics are embedded in how visual durations are reproduced.

articles.title: Cardiac and Respiratory Dynamics Modulate Temporal Interval Judgments
articles.authors: Amir Jahanian Najafabadi; Khaled Bagh; Kayser Christoph
articles.abstract: Judgments of time intervals are usually studied as decisions made just based on external sensory information. However, various bodily signals continuously provide a rhythmic context in which judgements of time are made. Hence bodily states may bias encoding, maintenance, and decision processes about time. The present study examined whether cardiac and respiratory dynamics predict trial-level performance in temporal interval tasks. Young adult participants completed auditory and visual short/long interval-judgment tasks while electrocardiography (ECG) or respiration was recorded continuously. From the ECG we extracted heart rate, heart-rate variability (RMSSD), cardiac phase, and a binary systole-state around stimulus onset, stimulus offset, and response onset. From the respiration signal we estimated respiratory phase and cycle length. Using Mixed-effects models we tested whether physiological predictors improved the prediction of accuracy and response bias beyond interval duration alone. Cardiac dynamics were associated primarily with response bias: lower heart rate was linked to a greater likelihood of short responses, RMSSD predicted underestimation in an interval-dependent manner, and systole-state models improved fit in time-resolved analyses, especially for shorter intervals. Respiratory phase also predicted temporal decisions, with phase-dependent changes in both short-response bias and accuracy across task-relevant windows. Together, these findings suggest that temporal interval judgments are embedded within dynamic bodily states. Rather than acting as peripheral noise, cardiac and respiratory signals provide physiologically meaningful context for temporal cognition.

articles.title: The Impact of Complexity on Risky Choices: An Evidence Accumulation Account
articles.authors: Maohua Nie; Jörg Rieskamp; Sebastian Olschewski
articles.abstract:
Risky options often differ not only in outcomes and probabilities, but also in the cognitive demands required to evaluate them. Yet most theories of risky choice either ignore complexity or treat it as a static feature of the option, modeled as a utility discount or with heteroscedastic errors. We propose a process-level framework that explains how complexity shapes both choice and response time within an evidence-accumulation architecture. The framework assumes that complexity reduces the signal-to-noise ratio of evidence accumulation, making evaluation slower and choices less consistent, and that decision makers partly adapt to these processing constraints by adjusting their decision strategies. These mechanisms can explain how complexity reduces choice consistency and how it shifts preferences toward simpler options.
We evaluated this framework in three preregistered experiments that manipulated complexity in structurally distinct ways: through the number of outcomes, arithmetic expressions of outcomes, and compound probabilities. Across studies, complexity made choices slower and less consistent. When both options were complex, these effects were best explained by reduced signal-to-noise ratios and partially compensatory increases in decision thresholds. When options differed in complexity, preferences for simpler options were best explained by an initial bias toward simplicity combined with a drift-rate adjustment during accumulation. The compound-probability manipulation, however, marked a boundary condition: different forms of complexity can change the representations that evidence accumulation operates on. Together, these findings advance a dynamic account of risky choice in which complexity shapes preference construction by changing both the rate at which decision evidence accumulates and the strategies used to evaluate the options.

articles.title: When Is Complexity Avoided in Risky Choice? A Domain Comparison of Gains and Losses
articles.authors: Maohua Nie; Jörg Rieskamp; Sebastian Olschewski
articles.abstract: Risky options often differ not only in expected value and risk but also in complexity. Although complexity aversion is well documented in the gain domain, it remains unclear whether this aversion extends to losses. We contrast two theoretical accounts that make diverging predictions: if complex options are avoided because processing them requires cognitive effort, complexity aversion should be similar for gains and losses; if complexity instead induces cognitive uncertainty, whose evaluation depends on domain-specific risk preferences, complexity aversion should be weaker for losses than for gains. We tested these predictions in two preregistered experiments (N = 138 and 135) using gambles that vary outcome complexity, separately for the gain and loss domain: Study 1 examined choices between two risky options, and Study 2 contrasted a risky with a sure option. In both studies, participants chose complex options significantly less often in the gain than in the loss domain; specifically, they were complexity averse for gains but complexity neutral for losses. Response times showed a converging asymmetry, significant in Study 2. Subjective ratings of cognitive uncertainty predicted complexity aversion in the gain but not in the loss domain. These results favor the cognitive-uncertainty account over the effort account: complexity increases cognitive uncertainty, whose behavioral consequences depend on the outcome domain.

articles.title: Modeling Individual Differences in Working Memory: Subject-Level Parameter Recovery within the Memory Measurement Model Framework (M³)
articles.authors: Jan; Gidon T. Frischkorn; Klaus Oberauer; Simon B. Schaefer; Anna-Lena Schubert
articles.abstract: The memory measurement model (M3) is a flexible modeling framework designed to measure parameters associated with different processes in working memory. It assumes that memory representations receive different levels of activation at retrieval, which arise from the sum of the strengths of item and binding memory. Transforming the activation of representations in different response categories into their respective recall probabilities then allows estimating the contributions of different memory processes to working memory performance. So far, parameter recovery has been reported only for group-level parameters of the M3. In contrast to experimental research, individual differences research focuses on variation in subject-level parameters. Adequate recovery of subject-level parameters is therefore a requirement for their valid measurement. To address this gap, we ran a parameter recovery simulation to assess subject-level parameter recovery as function of different experimental design choices. Our Bayesian hierarchical M3 implementation recovers subject parameters acceptably to very well, as demonstrated both through simulations and empirical parameter recovery using a complex span dataset. Based on the results, we recommend that researchers ensure that participants select not-presented lures (i.e., items not in the memory set) at least sometimes ( ≥ 2%) and collect a minimum of 200 retrieval responses per subject (40 trials at set size 5). When these conditions are met, the simple and complex span models specified in the M3 framework exhibit robust parameter recovery, well-calibrated posteriors, and satisfactory reliability. These challenges primarily arose from the substantial amount of data required to achieve sufficiently precise parameter estimates. In contrast, M3 parameters modeling free-time effects such as extended encoding and removal processes could not be recovered with sufficient precision and showed poor reliability. Posteriors of the M3-CS-EE model were well calibrated, while the M3-MU model showed systematic miscalibration of the subject-level parameters.

articles.title: Losing Focus Behind the Wheel: Psychometric Adaptation of the Attention‑Related Driving Errors Scale in Türkiye
articles.authors: Ibrahim Ozturk; Betül Akçakoca; Melike Kahraman; Alperen Orhan; Bahar Öz
articles.abstract: Understanding the psychosocial factors influencing driving behaviours is of significant importance due to its potential impact on enhancing road safety. A specific category of driving behaviours, attention-related driving errors, represents a critical yet understudied aspect of everyday road safety in Türkiye. To address this gap, this study aimed to (1) adapt the Attention-Related Driving Errors Scale (ARDES) for the Turkish context, (2) examine gender and in-vehicle interface differences in attention-related driving errors, and (3) investigate associations between attentional control, driving skills, and attention-related driving errors. A total of 420 licensed drivers (aged 18–62 years) participated in an online survey that included the ARDES, Attentional Control Scale, Driving Skills Inventory, and demographic measures. The sample was randomly divided for principal component analysis (PCA) and confirmatory factor analysis (CFA). Group differences were examined using the Kruskal–Wallis test, and the relationships between other factors and attention-related driving errors were tested via hierarchical regression. EFA supported a single-factor structure for the ARDES, explaining 32% of the variance, while CFA indicated an acceptable model fit. Female drivers reported significantly more attention-related errors than males, whereas males reported higher perceptual-motor skills. Interface type was associated only with attentional shifting, with drivers of combined interfaces scoring lower than those using touch- or button-based systems. Younger age, touch-based interface use, poorer attentional focus, and lower perceptual-motor and safety skills are associated with higher rates of attention-related driving errors. The results demonstrated that the ARDES-TR is a reliable and valid measure for assessing attention-related driving errors in Türkiye. These errors are significantly associated with attentional control and driving skills. These findings underscore the importance of considering both cognitive capacities and driving skills in interventions.

articles.title: Intra-decisional Dynamics Shape the Influence of Attributes on Value-based Choice
articles.authors: Douglas G. Lee; Fadong Chen; Youqi Quan
articles.abstract: Managers, marketers, and policymakers increasingly shape decisions by arranging when and how option attributes are presented, yet we lack a process-level account of why such interventions work. Do people apply well-defined preferences when making value-based decisions, or do they construct preferences on the spot in ways that depend on how information is acquired and evaluated over the course of a decision? Resolving this question is central to understanding and influencing decisions in households, organizations, and markets. Here, we investigate how the temporal dynamics of the choice process shape consumption decisions in two studies using response times and time manipulations. In each study, participants made binary choices between snack foods with and without time constraints. Using regression analysis and drift-diffusion modeling, we found that moving from time pressure to free response to time delay increases the importance of pleasure and decreases the importance of nutrition for pleasure-seeking participants, whereas the pattern reverses for nutrition-seeking participants. These results indicate that people preferentially process either pleasure or nutrition early in the choice process (relative to the other attribute) and that the time afforded by a choice environment systematically reweights these attributes. Because these intra-decisional dynamics are governed by when attributes enter processing, they identify a concrete lever – the ordering, salience, and timing of attribute information – through which managers and policymakers can steer consumption and other economic decisions.

articles.title: Anatomical Reorganisation Channels the Emergence of the Infant Vocal Repertoire
articles.authors: Christopher Martin Mikkelsen Cox; Axel G. Ekström
articles.abstract: Why do infants the world over begin their vocal lives with growls, grunts, squeals, and creaky phonation? And why does this pattern hold across radically different languages and caregiving environments? We propose that the mechanical geometry of the vocal tract at each developmental stage acts as a continuously changing constraint on what infant vocal exploration can discover. Beyond limiting what sounds are possible, this geometry actively generates certain acoustic events as the natural consequence of ordinary exploratory activity. In the neonatal larynx, tissue properties lower the thresholds for phonatory regime transitions; in the tongue, fibre geometry confines early exploration to a single axis until hyoid descent and palatal deepening open new dimensions; in the anterior articulators, independently available components, such as lip closure and jaw oscillation, await the reorientation of suprahyoid muscles that makes their coupling discoverable. Drawing on the motor development literature and neuropsychology of learning, we argue that vocal repertoire emerges through the same discover-stabilise-differentiate logic that governs early limb control: the body generates variation before any intent exists, sensory consequences draw the infant back to the patterns that produced them, and stabilised motor-auditory mappings gradually become communicative resources. The sequence of vocal development can thus be understood as the natural output of exploration within a continuously reorganising anatomy, where each new configuration, through its own mechanical properties, redefines the acoustic possibilities that undirected exploration will discover.

articles.title: Weak Links between Speech Perception and Speech Production at the Subphonemic Level
articles.authors: Brian W. L. Wong; Arthur G. Samuel; Efthymia C Kapnoula
articles.abstract: Recent research has shown individual differences in gradiency, defined as sensitivity to fine-grained acoustic differences at the subphonemic level. Consistency also varies, with some listeners providing more stable responses than others to repeated presentations of the same stimuli. However, it remains unclear whether gradiency and consistency are linked between perception and production. Across two experiments, 160 Spanish speakers completed a Visual Analogue Scale (VAS) task measuring perceptual gradiency and consistency along a Spanish /ba/–/pa/ continuum manipulated in 7–8 ms steps of voice onset time (VOT). The same participants also performed an explicit imitation task using the same stimuli. Results revealed only weak relationships between perceptual gradiency and imitation accuracy, as well as between perceptual consistency and imitation consistency, even after accounting for other factors related to speech perception and imitation. These findings suggest that models proposing strong perception–production coupling may not extend to the subphonemic level.

articles.title: The Impact of Social Learning on Learning Traps
articles.authors: Yanjun Liu; Alisha Shaikh; Ben R Newell; Andrew Perfors; Brett Hayes
articles.abstract: People often fall into learning traps where a false belief about the structure of the environment leads to under-exploration of rewarding options. Five studies (N = 1342) examined whether observation of decisions made by another learner facilitated escape from a trap or increased trap prevalence. In studies of horizontal social learning (Experiments 1a, 1b, 2), participants first had private experience with a task where approach of different category members could lead to gains or losses. We identified whether participants had learned an optimal two-dimensional categorization rule or fallen into the trap of using a one-dimensional rule. Participants then observed the approach decisions of another learner using the same or a different category rule. A substantial proportion of those who had initially fallen into the trap shifted to the optimal rule after observing use of an alternate rule. This escape from a learning trap was found following observation of both optimal (Experiment 1a) and sub-optimal rules (Experiment 1b, 2). In vertical social learning (Experiments 3, 4), social observation of approach decisions took place before private learning. Such observation led to reduced trap prevalence when the social demonstrator modeled an optimal rule but increased trap prevalence when they modeled a one-dimensional rule. These effects generalized to a learning environment with the same underlying feature structure but different feature-category mappings. These results both offer a novel approach to remediating learning traps as well as highlighting how poorly coordinated social learning can intensify traps.

articles.title: Gradual delays do not affect the tolerability of a smartphone friction intervention
articles.authors: Sabrina Fay Norwood; David Joachim Grüning; Frederik Riedel; Malte Elson
articles.abstract: Friction-based digital interventions reduce unwanted smartphone behaviour by interrupting automatic app-opening sequences, but substantial attrition rates limit their real-world impact. One proposed strategy for improving retention is to gradually increase intervention intensity, allowing users to adapt before encountering the full intervention dose. We tested this in a preregistered six-week field experiment (N = 1,641) in which new users of the smartphone friction app one sec were randomly assigned to one of four delay escalation schedules ranging from immediate full-dose exposure (10 seconds throughout) to gradual escalation (3 → 6 → 10 seconds). Retention was low and relatively similar across conditions (65–70% dropout), with no significant difference between any of three escalation schedules and the standard full-dose condition. Exploratory analyses likewise found no association between delay duration and weekly dropout. However, among participants who remained engaged, longer delays were associated with higher rates of dismissed app opening attempts, suggesting that delay duration influenced behaviour without improving retention. These findings do not support gradual intensity escalation as a retention strategy and instead suggest that intervention characteristics may optimise different outcomes. While delay duration appears useful for shaping behaviour among retained users, retention itself may depend more on the introduction of interruption than its precise duration.

articles.title: Training the power: Physical size guides the processing of exponential expressions
articles.authors: Bar Salman; Ami Feder; Serena Mingolo; Nadav Neumann; Mariya Lozin; Michal Pinhas
articles.abstract: This study examined how training and the physical size of base and power components affect the processing of exponential expressions. Research has shown that exponential expressions are cognitively challenging and that physical attributes, such as component size, can influence their processing. In the present study, we aimed to improve the comprehension of exponential expressions by training participants (N = 32) to learn the mathematical roles of bases and powers across standard and non-standard displays, where the latter featured a physically larger power than the base. Over five training sessions, participants practiced matching exponential expressions with their multiplication decompositions. In a subsequent test phase, we assessed both automatic processing (via a physical comparison task) and intentional processing (via a numerical comparison task) of the trained exponential expressions, as well as untrained expressions. Training improved response speed for familiar expressions, although automatic processing was limited; participants continued to focus on the physically larger component rather than the mathematically more important one. In the numerical comparison task, training improved the understanding of the power’s role for familiar expressions, but this understanding did not generalize to new expressions. Additionally, performance on the exponent knowledge test improved significantly following training, with reduced underestimation errors. The findings suggest that while training can enhance the intentional processing of exponential expressions, automatic processing of exponential syntax remains limited, highlighting the need for refined instructional approaches to exponential expressions.

articles.title: Recycling Rivalry: Social Identity Appeals Increase Recycling When Combined with Intergroup Comparison
articles.authors: Hege Landsvik; Jareef Martuza; Sveinung Jørgensen; Lars Jacob Pedersen; Siv Skard
articles.abstract: While many people recycle at home, they are less likely to do so in public, where high waste production meets a diffusion of individual responsibility. We examine whether social identity can close this gap. Across two preregistered season-long field experiments at a Norwegian Premier Division football stadium, we test the separate and combined effects of ingroup identity appeals and intergroup comparison on the recycling behavior of football supporters. In Study 1 (N = 5,712), an ingroup identity appeal did not increase recycling relative to an outgroup appeal, suggesting that standalone identity appeals are insufficient to shift behavior. When the ingroup appeal was combined with a ranking of clubs by their recycling rate, recycling rates were more than two times higher than in any other condition. Study 2 (N = 6,598) replicated this effect against a no-intervention control. Study 3 (N = 761), a post-game survey among Study 2’s participants, showed that supporters exposed to the combined intervention reported greater motivation to recycle and greater perceived importance of contributing to the ingroup’s success. These findings extend social identity theory by showing that identity appeals increase recycling when group performance is tied to a concrete metric of success, which an intergroup comparison can supply, making the behavior a way to pursue positive group distinctiveness.

articles.title: No Single Model Fits All: Conflict Decision-Making Models Vary More Across Datasets Than Across Tasks
articles.authors: Wanke Pan; Jia-Shun Wang; Klaus Oberauer; Hu Chuan-Peng
articles.abstract: Conflict variants of evidence accumulation models are widely used to explain human cognitive control. However, the generalizability of these models is largely unknown because of the lack of systematic comparisons across multiple conflict tasks and multiple datasets. Here, using a unified amortized Bayesian inference (ABI) framework, we compare the standard DDM and three conflict-specific variants across a benchmark database comprising eight independent studies (N = 1,375). We validate the ABI as a common framework for model comparison, fit DDM, DMC, DSTP, and SSP to each participant, and find that DSTP is the most frequently selected best-fitting model, but its superiority varies more across datasets than across tasks. Exploratory analyses show the 22 parameters cluster into four latent dimensions; the Inhibitory Process factor, of greatest theoretical interest in cognitive control, is unstable. Achieving cross-dataset generality of conflict diffusion models remains a major challenge.

articles.title: Depression symptom network reorganization under internet-based emotion regulation intervention: Evidence from a large real-world cohort
articles.authors: Jianjie Xu; Sihan Liu; Hanyi Zhang; lu Chen; Lv Xiangxi; Mengyu Miranda Gao; Yueqin Hu; Shaozheng Qin; Mark S. Chen; Rachel Han
articles.abstract: Depression can be conceptualized as a network of interacting symptoms. Although internet-based interventions are widely used, their associations with changes in symptom network structure remain unclear. Here, in a real-world observational cohort of 26,643 adults completing an internet-based emotion regulation intervention, we examined pre–post differences in depressive symptom network structure, global connectedness, and symptom centrality, stratified by reduction status. Analyses indicated that the two core depressive symptoms (i.e., depressed mood and anhedonia) showed reduced centrality after the intervention, whereas several non-core symptoms either increased or remained unchanged. The “symptom reduction” and “symptom non-reduction” subgroups showed largely comparable network characteristics at baseline. After the intervention, the “symptom reduction” subgroup displayed lower global network strength, a reorganized network topology, and reduced centrality of the core symptoms, whereas the “symptom non-reduction” subgroup showed no significant network alteration. Further analyses using residualized symptom change scores showed a similar pattern: among individuals with comparable baseline depressive symptom severity, those with better-than-expected outcomes showed lower post-intervention network connectivity than those with poorer-than-expected outcomes. Clinically anchored improvement analyses further indicated that reduced centrality of depressed mood was observed across alternative definitions of improvement. Although causal inference is precluded by the observational design, this study provides large-scale descriptive real-world evidence on how depressive symptom networks change alongside symptom reduction during routine use of a digital intervention.

articles.title: Empirically derived phenotypes can reduce diagnostic heterogeneity
articles.authors: Miriam K. Forbes; John F. Buss; Daniel P. Moriarity; Eiko I Fried; Holly Frances Levin-Aspenson; Lorenzo Lorenzo-Luaces; Kasey Stanton; Ashley L. Watts; Gregory W. Forbes
articles.abstract: Diagnostic heterogeneity is a longstanding challenge for the classification of mental illness because people who receive the same diagnosis can differ markedly in their symptom presentations as well as in the mechanisms underlying those symptoms. High heterogeneity undermines both the clinical utility of diagnostic labels and the scientific accuracy of research that treats disorders as coherent constructs. In this study, we examined heterogeneity across six internalizing disorders (specific phobia, social anxiety disorder, agoraphobia, generalized anxiety disorder [GAD], major depressive disorder [MDD], and posttraumatic stress disorder [PTSD]) using three complementary approaches to quantifying heterogeneity: 1) descriptive heterogeneity (how many symptom profiles can theoretically satisfy the diagnostic criteria, and how many are observed in practice), 2) person-focused heterogeneity (whether diagnostic labels capture people with similar symptom presentations), and 3) construct-focused heterogeneity (whether diagnostic labels group symptoms with similar patterns of association with external validators). Analyses drew on subsamples from a large convenience sample with elevated psychopathology, predominantly from Australia and the USA (n = 14,762, mean [SD] age = 38.0 [18.0]; 55% women). Results showed that specific phobia was consistently the least heterogeneous; social anxiety disorder, agoraphobia, and GAD had mixed results; and MDD and PTSD were highly heterogeneous across all metrics. Notably, empirically derived phenotypes nested within each disorder substantively reduced heterogeneity relative to the DSM diagnoses. The study provides both a systematic multi-method approach to characterising different types of diagnostic heterogeneity, and a practical path toward more precise and informative constructs that can be implemented by rescoring existing data.

articles.title: Bilingualism and Cognitive Aging in Ethnically Diverse Older Adults: Cross-sectional and Longitudinal Evidence from HABS-HD
articles.authors: Lihua Xia; Kang Ren; Ina Demetriou; Kshipra Gurunandan; Karin Meeker; Didac Vidal Pineiro; Richard Henson
articles.abstract:
Objectives
Identifying modifiable factors that shape cognitive aging trajectories is a central goal in aging research. This study examined whether bilingualism is associated with dementia status and longitudinal cognitive decline, and whether associations vary by ethnicity or gender.
Methods
We analyzed Wave 7 data from the Health and Aging Brain Study—Health Disparities (HABS-HD), a longitudinal US cohort of adults aged ≥50 years. Bilingualism was defined by self-reported use of a second language. Cross-sectional analyses included 4,140 participants (1,013 bilinguals); longitudinal analyses included 1,760 participants (522 bilinguals) followed for up to four visits at approximately 2-year intervals. Outcomes were baseline dementia status and latent factor scores for executive function and episodic memory derived from 11 neuropsychological tests. Regression and linear mixed-effects models assessed associations, adjusting for age, education, gender, ethnicity and practice effects.
Results
Results indicated that bilingualism was not associated with baseline dementia status or conversion to probable dementia. Cross-sectionally, associations varied by ethnicity: Hispanic bilinguals showed higher executive function and episodic memory scores. No advantage was seen in White participants; conversely, Black bilinguals had lower episodic memory scores. Longitudinally, bilingualism was associated with slower episodic memory decline independent of sociodemographic factors; no longitudinal association was observed for executive function. Discussion
These findings suggest that bilingualism may confer domain-specific benefits for memory trajectories in later life, while cross-sectional differences appear shaped by sociocultural context. The results underscore the importance of considering ethnic diversity and language history when evaluating experiential influences on cognitive aging.

articles.title: ‘It is my life don’t take that choice from me’: Autistic young adults’ experiences, preferences and needs regarding autistic peer support
articles.authors: Tohid Zarei; Caelan Farr; Maxx Fischer; Summer Marchiori; KJ Hepworth; Caroline Ellison; Tobias Loetscher
articles.abstract: Autistic peer support, as a two-way system of help, is uniquely positioned to address high rates of loneliness and mental health challenges among autistic young adults. We aimed to inform the development of autistic peer support programs aligned with participants’ preferences and needs through a mixed methods online survey study. A total of 73 autistic young adults (aged 18-30; 34 women, 19 non-binary, 11 men, 7 transgender men, 1 transgender woman, 1 undisclosed) completed a survey covering peer interactions, peer support preferences and needs, as well as delivery preferences. While following participatory research processes, we used reflexive thematic analysis to identify an overarching theme: flying together through shared understanding and shared struggles. This maps onto participants’ desire for reciprocal connections that enable understanding and safe unmasking, and their preference for in-person programs adapted to a range of support needs with meaningful participation in decision-making. Autistic Burnout and social connection were most participants’ preferred areas to be addressed. Especially when co-produced or peer-led, autistic peer support programs can contribute to providing a sense of collective movement with preserved self-determination for participants.

articles.title: Beyond Reciprocity: Common Knowledge of Social Identity Enhances the Intrinsic Value of Ingroup Coopertion
articles.authors: Onyul Haque; Leor M Hackel
articles.abstract: People are often more willing to help or cooperate with members of their own groups as opposed to other groups. This prosociality could reflect intrinsic value placed on acts of ingroup cooperation or a strategic expectation that ingroup members will cooperate more and provide tangible gains. A key line of evidence for the strategic view is that people show more ingroup favoritism when both parties are aware of shared group membership, which means they can each expect more favorable treatment. However, common knowledge of shared identity may also make interactions feel more meaningful. Here, we provide evidence that the effects of membership knowledge need not reflect strategic expectations alone but can also reflect the intrinsic value of ingroup cooperation. Across three experiments, participants played multiple one-shot trust games with ingroup and outgroup trustees. For each trust decision, participants were aware of the exact proportion of times trustees from a given group had reciprocated trust; this likelihood of reciprocity was held constant between ingroup and outgroup trustees. Although expectations of reciprocity were thus known and held constant, participants preferred to trust ingroup members over outgroup members, and this bias was amplified when participants believed trustees knew about their shared group membership. These results suggest that ingroup members cooperate more when they are aware of each other’s social identity not only because it increases their expectations of obtaining tangible gains but also because it boosts the intrinsic social value of cooperating with a fellow ingroup member.

articles.title: Recovery order in adaptive systems is set by dependency structure
articles.authors: Hiroki Saito
articles.abstract: Adaptive systems recover their capacities in reproducible orders. Predicting it has meant fitting a dynamical model to each system and reading the order off its trajectories, an output of the fit, not of structure. Here we show that recovery order follows from dependency structure: which capacities must be in place before which others recover. From four axioms we prove that where prerequisite gates vanish at baseline no capacity begins to recover before its prerequisites, whatever the rate constants, and that under a common deficit-closing rule with rates non-increasing along dependencies the admissible orders are exactly the linear extensions of the graph: a chain gives a unique sequence, a branch a partial order. We map where steep heterogeneity adds further orders. The graph is an input, realized in probabilistic models as identifiability structure. We instantiate it in catatonia, post-injury motor recovery and curriculum learning, the last without a probabilistic model.

articles.title: The Saito Loop, a computational theory of hierarchical recovery in catatonia
articles.authors: Hiroki Saito
articles.abstract: Clinical observation identified a reproducible recovery hierarchy in catatonia, the Saito Loop (πs → β → πm → πv_fast → πv_slow), but not why recovery should follow any fixed order. We ask whether the order follows from an active-inference architecture without being supplied. The five computational quantities follow a priori from their computational roles; structural identifiability analysis then reconstructs their prerequisite relations as a directed acyclic graph. Because the graph is a chain, its topological ordering is unique and identical to the Saito Loop: the order is a structural consequence of the dependency relations, not a fitted sequence, and the complete ordering is never supplied. All uniqueness claims hold within an explicitly specified model class, and whether the structural order is realized in recovery time is a separate, falsifiable dynamical question. The clinically observed recovery hierarchy therefore becomes a constrained computational consequence rather than an empirical regularity.

articles.title: Characterizing the functional characteristics/rules governing extended cognition during conversation
articles.authors: Zachary P Rosen
articles.abstract: The study of extended cognition encompasses individuals' ability to come together as a group to solve complex problems -- often with greater processing power than is available to any one person alone. Research in this area has pointed to conversation as an integral component of extended cognitive processes. However, if conversation acts as a crucial support for extended cognition it needs to be able to enact certain functions to do so. The current study deploys a hybrid information-theoretic and language modeling framework to analyze a dataset of 5,447 conversations across nine different languages in order to ascertain the computational rules that allow speakers and their partners to generate new information relative to what they have expressed in prior turns -- a key part of extended cognition. We conclude by providing a set of rules governing how speakers form an extended cognitive system, finely tuned for jointly creating new content from old ideas.

articles.title: Theory of Mind and Body: Interoceptive Accuracy Predicts Accurate Intuitions of Another’s Internal State
articles.authors: Asa Young; Hana M. Ibarra; Zenon A. Demko; Max Granholm; Jonathan Schooler
articles.abstract: Empathy is often conceptualized as an inferential process in which perceivers estimate another’s internal state by integrating observable cues with referential models. Because psychophysiological states are accompanied by changes in both behavior and physiology, interoceptive accuracy may support inferences about another’s internal state. We tested whether interoceptive accuracy predicts alteroceptive accuracy: the ability to estimate another person’s bodily state. In Experiment 1 (n = 67), participants completed the Heartbeat Counting task and a structurally homologous alteroceptive task in which they estimated a co-participant’s heartbeats by observation alone. Alteroceptive performance exceeded empirical chance and interoceptive accuracy predicted alteroceptive accuracy. Experiment 2 (n = 75) showed that this association was not explained by interval timing, heart rate beliefs, or heart rate similarity. Exploratory analyses suggested that alteroceptive accuracy uniquely predicted alexithymia, decision making under uncertainty, and emotion recognition. A theory of body may provide a tractable substrate upon which a theory of mind is constructed.

articles.title: Shared Identity and Felt Understanding in the Context of Sexual Minority Stress:  Who Gets Me, and Why?
articles.authors: Emma Laurel McGorray; Khava Gillespie; Elsie Newburg; Eli Finkel
articles.abstract: Although sexual minority stress often predicts lower well-being, LGBQ+ people may be protected against these effects if they receive support that helps them feel understood. What processes are linked to greater felt understanding? Across four studies, we tested the hypothesis that LGBQ+ people feel more understood by LGBQ+ (vs. heterosexual) support providers and tested two possible explanations for this relationship: (1) LGBQ+ support providers offer higher-quality support (the support quality explanation) and (2) people’s beliefs about shared identity are linked to how they evaluate support (the interpretive filter explanation). Using varied methodologies—participants reflecting on their close relationships and evaluating both genuine and experimentally manipulated support messages—we found limited evidence for the former explanation but more robust evidence for the latter. These findings underscore the power of sharing an identity with a support provider when experiencing minority stress, while also suggesting that mere beliefs about shared identity may be a major source of that power.

articles.title: Which Comes First: Ideology, or Moral Values? Panel evidence from the 2024 U.S. Presidential Election
articles.authors: Pierce D. Ekstrom; Kevin Smith; Ingrid Johnsen Haas; John Jostes
articles.abstract: Recent work has called into question the longstanding intuition that differences in political orientation are attributable to differences in moral values; instead, people may change their reported values to justify their political preferences. To identify which most plausibly causes which, we conducted a three-wave panel study, using quotas to approximate a demographically representative initial sample of U.S. adults and measuring values in four different ways, with each measure grounded in a distinct theoretical framework. We found that: 1) Ideology and partisanship consistently showed greater cross-wave stability than values. 2) Within-subject wave-to-wave shifts in political orientation and values were rarely and weakly related in either direction. Between-subjects analyses replicated existing work: conservatives and liberals tended to value different things. But during these months, respondents did not tend to become more conservative or liberal depending on what they valued, or to come to value anything more or less because of their ideology.

articles.title: Is fashion just a fashion? Or does it have an evolutionary basis?
articles.authors: Rudiger von der Heydt
articles.abstract: Female models presented in advertising, entertainment, and fashion shows are much slimmer on average than the general population. The fashion industry has been criticized for advertising a body type that would influence the self perception of young women, leading to eating disorders and concomitant health risks. Given the intense criticism one would expect a corresponding change in publication policies that would mitigate these negative effects. But a recent study that analyzed 25 years of published fashion records found no improvement. The present paper suggests an evolutionary explanation for why consumers prefer the unrealistic body type.

articles.title: Stimulated recall protocols: Field-specific guidelines for second language acquisition and bilingualism research
articles.authors: John Dylan Burton; Soyoung Lim; Sneha Samuvel
articles.abstract: Stimulated recall protocols are one of the most popular methods in second language acquisition and bilingualism research to investigate language learners’ internal thought processes when using second languages. Although methodological handbooks are available for learning how to set up a stimulated recall study, there is little empirically driven guidance on best practices for reporting variables central to the method. To develop field-specific reporting guidelines, this systematic review analyzed articles that used stimulated recall to elicit introspective reports in sixteen Q1 journals in applied linguistics between 2000 and 2024. After screening, 171 studies were analyzed for 62 variables inherent to this practice. Findings showed that some details were well-reported, but others critical for stimulated recalls, such as the use of instructions or the L2 proficiency of participants, were reported infrequently. The review concludes with empirically derived reporting guidelines derived from the literature to support authors, editors, and peer reviewers.

articles.title: Artificial Intelligence Systems Distort Upstream Selection in Human Social Learning
articles.authors: William J. Brady; Chen-Wei Yu; Nicholas Ornstein; Bolun Sun; Joshua Conrad Jackson
articles.abstract: Humans are social learners who depend on observing others to acquire knowledge, norms, and behaviors, a capacity that underlies cumulative cultural evolution. Social learning unfolds in two stages: upstream selection determines what information becomes visible, and downstream selection determines what learners copy from that visible sample. Downstream selection occurs through biases such as conformity bias (copying what appears common) and prestige bias (copying those who appear highly respected). These downstream biases can be adaptive when upstream selection yields a sample that reflects the population's true distribution, so that what appears common is actually common and those who appear respected are actually competent. We argue that digital technologies disrupt this condition, creating an upstream selection problem. Engagement-based algorithms amplify the tails of the distribution, surfacing rare and extreme content, whereas generative AI collapses it toward the mode (of the population or the user), erasing the surrounding diversity. Crucially, in each system the optimization signal shapes both visibility and prestige. For engagement-based algorithms, the signal is engagement: creators who post extreme content become more visible and, through the likes, shares, and followers, appear more prestigious. For generative AI, the signal is statistical typicality: it makes a modal answer dominant and, with no alternatives shown, makes the model that produced it appear more prestigious. These distortions can give rise to emergent group-level phenomena, including pluralistic ignorance and illusory consensus. Synthesizing evidence across psychology, cultural evolution, and computational social science, we provide a framework for how digital technologies disrupt social learning and outline interventions for restoring functional cultural transmission.

articles.title: The Impact of Sycophantic AI on Attitudes and Decisions
articles.authors: Steve Rathje; Meryl Ye; Laura K. Globig; Raunak M Pillai; Victoria Oldemburgo de Mello; Jerry Chen; Jay Joseph Van Bavel
articles.abstract: There is widespread concern that AI chatbots are “sycophantic,” or overly agreeable and validating. However, less is known about the causal impact of interacting with sycophantic AI on beliefs and behaviors. Across seven studies (total n = 7,227), we found that people enjoyed interacting with sycophantic AI chatbots more than interacting with neutral chatbots or “disagreeable” chatbots that challenged them. Brief conversations with sycophantic chatbots about political or personal topics increased the strength of people’s attitudes. However, popular AI models not prompted to be sycophantic did not consistently change attitudes. Sycophantic chatbots also inflated people’s perceptions that they were better than the average person on desirable traits (e.g., intelligence, empathy), and also led people to bet more money that they scored better than average on tasks purporting to measure desirable traits. Participants consistently rated sycophantic chatbots as more “unbiased” than disagreeable chatbots, even though third-party raters viewed these chatbots as equally biased, suggesting that people may be blind to biases in AI output that aligns with their views. Altogether, these results suggest that sycophantic model behavior can entrench attitudes and lead to overconfident beliefs and decisions. Despite this, people enjoy sycophantic models and often fail to recognize their biases.

articles.title: Pilot Study of Combined tDCS and Cognitive Training Intervention for Suicide Risk with Ecological Momentary Assessment: Feasibility and Acceptability in Psychiatric Inpatient Veterans
articles.authors: Katherine Hein; Beryl Palmer; Brooke Bjerke; Carol Chu; Casey Gilmore
articles.abstract:
Objective: This pilot study examined the feasibility and acceptability of an impulsivity-targeted neuromodulation intervention and high-density ecological momentary assessment (EMA) in high-risk veterans with suicidal thoughts and behaviors following discharge from acute inpatient psychiatric care.
Method: Fourteen adult veterans receiving acute psychiatric care screened for suicide risk were recruited to the study and completed a baseline assessment, 10 sessions of transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) paired with cognitive training, one month of EMA surveys (2-3x per day) post-discharge, and questionnaires and cognitive tasks one- and two-months following the last intervention received.
Results: Study feasibility was supported by a 21% enrollment rate, 56% intervention adherence, and no reported difficulties tolerating the intervention. Adherence to EMA surveys was high (77%) among participants who completed the EMA protocol, with the highest adherence in the first week followed by a reduction in subsequent weeks.
Conclusions: This study demonstrated that neuromodulation and cognitive training interventions and high-density EMA designs are generally feasible and acceptable among veterans at high risk of suicide following acute psychiatric care. Recommendations for increasing feasibility and adherence to such interventions and suicide risk safety procedures for intensive EMA protocols with high-risk veterans are discussed.

articles.title: “We love our jobs!” Systems Thinking and Participatory Action Research for the future of neurodiversity and skilled employment
articles.authors: Dora M Raymaker; Shawna Spain; Nybelle Caruso; Joelle Maslak; Nicole Leblanc; Morénike Giwa Onaiwu; Jonathan Spector; Passion Ilea; Julia Crown; Kristin Akervall
articles.abstract: Although neurodivergent people can achieve high levels of academic and vocational training in the same professions as others, they remain un- and under-employed; this is in part due to the “wickedness” of the problem. To address the complexity we convened a group of neurodivergent lived experience and employment experts to  1) define which problems in neurodiversity and skilled employment are most urgent to address; 2) create actionable strategies with potential leverage for generating the desired employment outcomes. We used qualitative methods from the systems thinking field: Soft Systems Methodology, futures visioning and SWOT analysis, and Group Model Building (system dynamics). The workshops resulted in identifying intervention leverage between organizational psychology constructs of employee wellbeing, workplace climate, and mutually beneficial workplace relationships, in conjunction with a new disability stress construct, rather than specific skills building or remediation of disability characteristics. Reaching a future in which neurodivergent people love their jobs will take education, resources, champions from the outside and inside, universal access, paradigm shifts, infrastructure, and recognition of individual and social complexity. We recommend examining the organizational psychology literature for adaptable interventions; focusing on peer support; leveraging emerging technology to manage complexity; and supporting supervisor behavior change based on authentic understanding.

articles.title: Sensory Saturation and Cognitive Surrender: A Theoretical Framework for Altered Perceptual States in Immersive Neurogastronomic Dining
articles.authors: Federico Rottigni; Stelios Kiosses
articles.abstract: This paper proposes a theoretical framework for interpreting immersive neurogastronomic experiences as a form of ambient cognitive modulation. The framework originates in the direct, informal observation of approximately 6,000 guests conducted by the first author over more than six years of operation at Sensorium — an eleven-seat neurogastronomic restaurant with a controlled multisensory architecture. The recurrence of consistent behavioural and experiential patterns across this substantial case base motivated a search for a systematic neurological and psychological interpretation, developed in collaboration with the second author drawing on his clinical expertise and the Emotional Flavour Profiles framework (Kiosses, 2026). We propose that intentional, layered sensory overstimulation may selectively inhibit dominant analytical processing — in the sense described by McGilchrist's account of hemispheric functional dominance — and reduce Default Mode Network (DMN) activity, favouring a shift in brain oscillatory states from alpha toward theta. This hypothesised neurobiological shift, potentially observable within the span of a single dining session, may correspond to a subjective experience of heightened presence, reduced critical self-monitoring, and access to ordinarily unavailable inner states. We introduce a three-stage model — Saturation, Analytical Surrender, and Incorporeal Immersion — and discuss its implications for experiential design, clinical psychology, and wellbeing research.

articles.title: Pupil size dynamics predict momentary changes in self-reported arousal
articles.authors: Ryan Yan Yan; Tara Srirangarajan; Jeremy Bailenson; Brian Knutson
articles.abstract: Subjective arousal, or feelings of activation and alertness, can dynamically modulate affect, behavior, and cognition. Momentary changes in subjective arousal have typically been assessed with self-report in humans, which may alter those very feelings. Although researchers have traditionally used pupil size as a physiological index of arousal, links between pupil dynamics and momentary changes in subjective arousal remain unclear. Here, we combined continuous pupillometry with repeated self-report probes of changing arousal as individuals engaged in a modified Monetary Incentive Delay task. Across Virtual Reality (N = 28; 12 females, 16 males) and Functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging (N = 27; 15 females, 12 males) studies, tonic and phasic pupil measures jointly predicted subsequent self-reported arousal beyond stated incentive value and at a temporal lag of approximately 1.5–3.5 seconds. Neural activity associated with pupil dynamics further predicted pupil size, self-reported arousal, and behavioral motivation in held-out data. Together, these convergent findings establish pupil size as a temporally-precise marker of momentary fluctuations in self-reported arousal.

articles.title: Imagination boosts strategy learning
articles.authors: Jack Burgess; Timothy D. Verstynen
articles.abstract: Imagination is thought to boost exploration and problem solving by simulating states that have not been directly experienced as a means of reasoning through future plans. Here we tested this idea in the context of an impartial combinatorial game with a ground truth optional strategy. Adopting a stumbler-strategist reinforcement learning architecture, we showed how imagination can boost optimal strategy learning over memory replay. These model predictions were validated experimentally in humans (N=255) using an intervention design where participants were tasked with either imagining unplayed scenarios, reviewing prior games, or engaging in a simple visual attention task (control). These convergent results show how imagination uniquely boosts strategy learning in partially explored tasks.

articles.title: FLM UNGOAL: A Factor-Label Method for Removing Semantic Distractors in Health Behavior Change
articles.authors: Mohsen Dolatabadi
articles.abstract:
Health behavior change frequently fails despite genuine patient motivation and adequate health literacy. This article presents a proof-of-concept single-subject case study (N=1) investigating the FLM UNGOAL framework—a novel cognitive-identity restructuring protocol using the Factor-Label Method (dimensional analysis) to systematically remove ungoal distractors (maladaptive Past Self cognitions in QIII) and transfer identity to the Future I (QI) via a diagonal conversion vector through a 4-region trigonometric spatial architecture.
Participant: A 42-year-old bilingual Persian-Iranian male (native Persian, fluent German) with Type 2 Diabetes (HbA1c 8.2%) and poor treatment adherence. Procedure: Following a 7-day baseline, the participant engaged in 6 sessions (90 min each) over 6 weeks using the FLM UNGOAL Board and protocol. Measures: Tri-Circle Overlap Index (TCOI), Goal Proximity Index (GPI), Conversion Factor (CF), daily practice logs. Results: TCOI improved from 0.18 (baseline, high Past Self identification) to 3.00 (post-intervention, Future I dominant) to 5.67 (maintenance). GPI increased from 15% to 85%. CF increased from N/A to 5.7. HbA1c improved from 8.2% to 7.0% at 3-month follow-up. Qualitative reports confirmed reduced cognitive friction and sustained identity transfer.
The framework integrates embodied cognition (Lakoff & Johnson, 1999), the Tri-Circle Temporal Self Model (Markus & Nurius, 1986; Higgins, 1987), industrial design principles via the FLM UNGOAL Board, complex systems theory, and Measurement-Based Care principles (Fortney et al., 2017). The 4-region trigonometric circle maps valence (Y-axis: Positive/Negative) and temporality (X-axis: Future/Past) with Cartesian independence—Fear is precisely localized to QIV (Future + Negative) and deliberately bypassed by the diagonal conversion vector. The protocol captures any representational format (pure shape, pure proposition, or hybrid) and transforms it through spatial reconfiguration alone.
This proof-of-concept offers initial empirical support for the FLM UNGOAL framework while charting a clear course for rigorous replication and randomized controlled trials.

articles.title: Neurodivergence, Physical Activity and Sport: Challenging Neuro-Normativity and Advancing the Field
articles.authors: Patrick Jachyra; Robert Townsend
articles.abstract: Neurodivergence is a fast-emerging area of interest in sport and physical activity (PA), yet research remains dominated by biomedical assumptions and deficit-based framings. This chapter outlines two contrasting perspectives on neurodivergence - the medical model and the neurodiversity paradigm - and examines how these shape understandings of participation across the lifespan. We illustrate how sensory, social, structural, and socioeconomic barriers restrict neurodivergent people’s engagement in sport and PA and argue that these exclusions reflect broader systems of ableism, disablism, and neuro-normativity embedded within sport. We reflexively interrogate how neuro normative assumptions are reproduced in sport and PA arenas by drawing on our research experience. We conclude by outlining a research agenda grounded in neurodivergent justice, calling for neurodivergent led methodologies, critical interrogation of sport’s normative environments, challenging neuro-ableism and a shift from individualised interventions to structural transformation. We ask, what if barriers are not individual shortcomings, but limits of the human imagination.

articles.title: Addiction as a Chronic Brain Disease: A Narrative Review of the Neurobiological Evidence
articles.authors: David Olaleye
articles.abstract:
Addiction has traditionally been explained in moral terms, as a failure of discipline repeated one
too many times. Three decades of neuroscience research complicate that story considerably.
Repeated exposure to alcohol and other drugs changes how the brain's reward circuitry responds
to everyday experience, weakens the prefrontal systems responsible for planning and impulse
control, and leaves behind changes to stress and memory circuits that can persist long after drug
use has stopped. This narrative review draws on major research syntheses, including work by
Volkow, Koob, and colleagues and Heilig and colleagues' 2021 reassessment of the brain disease
model, to lay out the neurobiological case for classifying addiction as a chronic brain disease. It
also takes seriously the strongest published objections to that framing, including Sally Satel and
Scott Lilienfeld's argument that a heavily biological account can understate the role of choice and
context, Gene Heyman's evidence on unassisted recovery, and experimental work showing that a
disease-focused message can reduce people's stated intent to seek treatment. The review
concludes that the neurobiological evidence is substantial enough to support the disease
classification, but that the classification works best when paired with, rather than substituted for,
personal responsibility and psychosocial treatment. It closes with a discussion of clinical and
1 policy implications and the limits of a narrative review built on a curated set of sources rather
than a systematic literature search.

articles.title: Hate Speech versus Free Speech: How Online Hate Speech Shapes Perceptions and Regulatory Preferences about Freedom of Expression
articles.authors: Cornelia Sindermann; Eva-Maria Trüdinger
articles.abstract: While social media platforms have expanded avenues for social and political engagement and self-expression, they are also spheres for hateful online speech. This contrast has intensified debates about how to reconcile the protection of free speech with efforts to regulate hate speech. Yet, causal evidence on how the presentation and related perceptions of online hate speech affect citizens’ perceptions of freedom of expression and regulatory preferences in view of this dilemma remains scarce. To address this gap, we conducted a preregistered online experiment with two independent samples from the German population (total N = 1,045). Participants were randomly assigned to view hate speech targeting different political groups across two issue domains (climate change, LGBTQIA+ rights), factual information on the respective issue, or no stimulus. Then, they provided information on the perceived incivility of the stimuli and their attitudes toward freedom of expression. We show that mere exposure to hate speech does not significantly affect the perceived state of freedom of expression or regulatory preferences. However, individuals who perceive hate speech as more uncivil are more likely to favor combating hate speech over protecting freedom of expression. This finding points to the importance of individual perceptions of harmful content when assessing its social and political consequences.

articles.title: Bilingual experience predicts language skills, but not reading skills, in a low-literacy and multilingual context
articles.authors: Mary-Claire Ball; Natasha Vujičić; Armand Yeboue; Micaela Ostry; Amy Ogan; Sharon Wolf; Kaja Kinga Jasińska
articles.abstract: Children throughout the world attend school and learn to read in a language of instruction (LoI) other than the language(s) they speak at home, which is one factor contributing to poor reading outcomes. Understanding reading development in multilingual, Majority World contexts is important for improving reading skills globally. In a linguistically diverse sample of children in rural Côte d’Ivoire, we examined how home language experience (monolingual, regional bilingual [two Ivorian languages], French bilingual [French + Ivorian language], French multilingual [French + two Ivorian languages]) relates to children’s (N = 1335) language and reading skills. Bilingual children (French and regional) outperformed monolingual children on French language tasks, suggesting bilingual experience benefits language skills regardless of whether it includes the LoI (French). However, this language advantage did not extend to reading; there were no differences in reading scores between groups and all children leveraged phonological awareness for reading regardless of their home language experience. The findings suggest that bilingual/multilingual education programs, and reading instruction that strengthens language skills, may support reading outcomes in multilingual, Majority World contexts.

articles.title: Personality trait and state associations with cognitive functioning and variability in middle and older adults
articles.authors: Winkie Ma; Adam Taylor Nissen; Zoe Hawks; Eileen Kranz Graham; Dan Mroczek; Emorie D Beck
articles.abstract: Personality characteristics are early indicators of later cognitive functioning, but existing studies primarily focused on trait-level trends. How well these between-person differences translate to risk-mitigating interventions remains unclear. Addressing this entails examining within-person differences that explain how states may accumulate over time to influence longer-term outcomes. The present study answers this by investigating associations between personality traits and states and momentary cognitive function and variability. We conducted a three-week ecological momentary assessment study of middle and older adults (N = 183). We used Bayesian Mixed-Effect Location Scale Models to capture contingencies between personality and momentary cognitive functioning and variability. We additionally explored machine learning via (elastic net regression) profiles of personality state-cognition contingencies to identify who experiences stronger associations. At the trait-level, higher conscientiousness was associated with poorer working memory and processing speed. Higher openness was associated with better cognitive functioning and lower variability for episodic memory and processing speed. At the state-level, conscientiousness was better for working memory performance, while neuroticism was associated with variable episodic memory functioning. Extraversion was associated with working and episodic memory functioning and variability. Finally, sociodemographic, health, and personality trait variables emerged as top predictors of individual differences in within-person associations. By investigating within-person associations between personality and cognitive ability, we demonstrate that trait-level associations do not necessarily generalize to state-level ones. Profiles of top predictors of individual differences in state-level associations may be promising targets for intervention, but interventions should be tailored with between- and within-person differences in mind.

articles.title: Sparse Residual Estimation in Partially Confirmatory Factor Analysis
articles.authors: Jin Yi; Jinsong Chen; Zi Yan; Ying Zhang
articles.abstract:
This article extends the Bayesian regularized variational procedure for partially confirmatory factor analysis to accommodate sparse residual dependence. Existing PCFA-VA assumes a diagonal residual covariance, which may be restrictive in practice. Using continuous spike-and-slab priors, the proposed method jointly selects factor loadings and residual dependence structures while allowing available expert knowledge to be incorporated. It spans a broad confirmatory-exploratory continuum, accommodating fully or partially specified loading structures with residual dependence selection and fully unspecified loading structures with partially specified residual dependence. Rather than relying on stochastic posterior sampling, we develop a variational expectation conditional maximization (VECM) algorithm for posterior approximation and estimation. By varying the scale of the spike densities along a regularization path, the algorithm supports dynamic model exploration and progressively removes negligible loadings and residual dependence relations. Simulations demonstrate the framework's flexibility under diagonal and non-diagonal residual structures. When residual dependence is absent, it retains PCFA-VA as a special case and yields lower estimation error. When residual dependence is present, it achieves structure recovery and estimation accuracy comparable to the MCMC-based PCFA method, at markedly lower computational cost. An empirical application further illustrates that the loading and residual dependence structures selected by VECM are substantively interpretable. }
\keywords{factor analysis, residual dependence, spike-and-slab, variational inference

articles.title: Acceptability of a Virtual Reality and Artificial Intelligence Enhanced Exposure and Response Prevention Therapy Platform for Treating Obsessive Compulsive Disorder
articles.authors: Eddie Silber; Arlen C. Moller
articles.abstract:
Introduction: Exposure and response prevention (ERP) is the gold standard treatment for obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), yet its reach and effectiveness are limited by barriers related to clinician training, patient engagement, and symptom heterogeneity. Emerging technologies, including virtual reality (VR) and generative artificial intelligence (GenAI), may help address these limitations. However, clinician perspectives on integrating these technologies into ERP remain largely unexplored.

Methods: This pilot study used a cross-sectional mixed-methods design. Eight clinical psychology doctoral trainees participated in a demonstration of a combined VR and GenAI (VR-Gen-AI) exposure therapy platform, followed by semi-structured interviews and a survey. Interview data were thematically analyzed by two independent coders.

Findings: Clinicians identified several potential benefits, including immersive exposure experiences, personalized stimulus generation, and the potential to bridge imaginal and in vivo exposures. Participants also perceived greater treatment engagement. Reported concerns included image quality, physical side effects, and the potential for VR to reinforce compulsive behaviors if implemented inappropriately. Participants emphasized the importance of active therapist involvement and careful assessment of client suitability.

Discussion: Findings support emerging literature suggesting that VR and GenAI may enhance the personalization and delivery of ERP while highlighting important implementation considerations.

Limitations: The small sample of doctoral trainees and brief demonstration outside a clinical setting may limit generalizability.

Conclusions: VR-GenAI represents a promising adjunct to ERP. Future research should evaluate its effectiveness with OCD specialists and patients using controlled clinical trials.

articles.title: Beyond awareness: A multidimensional meta-analysis on the nuanced relationship between interoception and emotion regulation
articles.authors: Emma Casey; Anna Sofia Sofia Caruso; Seth Kaplan; Cydney Kennedy; Timothy Curby; Thalia R Goldstein
articles.abstract: Interoception—the processes by which one senses, interprets, integrates, and regulates signals arising from within the body—is theorized to be central to emotional experience and its regulation. Research examining the interoception–emotion regulation relationship has grown rapidly over the past decade, yet findings remain difficult to synthesize, in part due to the multidimensional nature of both constructs, the variety of ways in which each is measured. We conducted a multilevel meta-analysis of 52 publications (71 samples, 1,353 effect sizes, N = 10,123) examining associations between domains of interoception and emotion regulation. Although the overall pooled effect was small, a nuanced and patterned set of associations emerged when dimension and measurement approach were considered. Associations were stronger for trait than state measures of emotion regulation, and for self-reported than performance-based measures of interoception. Among interoceptive dimensions, metacognitive aspects, including appraisals of bodily sensations and attentional control over interoceptive awareness, were more strongly associated with emotion regulation than awareness of bodily signals alone. Associations also differed meaningfully in samples characterized by neurodivergence and eating atypicalities. These findings highlight the importance of distinguishing among dimensions of interoceptive processing when examining its relationship to emotion regulation, and point to appraisal and attentional control as particularly promising targets for future research and clinical intervention.

articles.title: Learning to Care More About Distant Others:  A Systematic Moral Reflection Intervention
articles.authors: Charlotte Riedl; Tao Burga; Erola Pons; Patricia Groß; Falk Lieder
articles.abstract: People's willingness to help others declines steeply with social distance: the more distant, different, or stigmatized those in need are, the less time, money, and consideration they receive — even when they need help the most. This article shows that moral learning from the consequences of past decisions can teach people to give more consideration to the welfare of outgroup members in future decisions and increase their outgroup prosociality. We developed a series of Socratic questions that guide people to systematically reflect on how their decision in a social dilemma affected distant others and how they reached it. Across four preregistered experiments (one reported in the Supplemental Materials), learning from a past decision through systematic moral reflection made participants more willing to donate their time and money to charities that help distant others, including real, incentive-compatible donations to charities helping a stigmatized group. Its effects transferred to outgroups the intervention never mentioned, persisted for more than one week, and exceeded those of two established prejudice-reduction interventions: empathy induction and perspective-taking. Process tracing methods and thematic analysis of the lessons participants learned indicated that these changes were mediated by participants learning to deliberate more and give greater consideration to how their actions affect distant others. These findings identify metacognitive learning as a promising pathway to expanding the reach of human generosity toward those who need it most.

articles.title: Seeing the world through others' minds: Determining the role of executive functions in social cognitive processes
articles.authors: Katerina Michalaki; Charlotte Rebecca Pennington; Stephen Mayhew; Klaus Kessler; Daniel Shaw
articles.abstract: Our ability to infer others’ mental states (e.g., perspectives and beliefs) is integral to successful social interaction. A long-standing debate is whether mentalising relies upon specialised social-cognitive processes or more domain-general systems that coordinate our thoughts and behaviour across social and non-social contexts. In this preregistered study, we investigated this directly by determining the causal links between mentalising and three supposedly distinct domain-general executive functions (EFs): interference resolution (the suppression of task-irrelevant information), set shifting (the flexible switching between cognitive states) and memory updating (using new information to update memory representations). A large sample (N=369) completed an online battery of three experimental tasks that measured each of the EFs and a fourth that measured mentalising – our ability to infer how the world appears from someone’s else viewpoint (level-2 visuospatial perspective-taking; VPT-2) and acknowledge that others’ belief about the world may align with or diverge from our privileged knowledge of reality (true- and false-belief reasoning). Two structural equation models were applied to data acquired with this battery to evaluate direct and indirect pathways between EFs and mentalising. Contrary to our hypotheses, these models suggest that better memory updating  and interference resolution increased the cognitive costs associated with VPT-2 and false-belief reasoning, respectively, while set shifting showed no significant effects on mentalising. Furthermore, VPT-2 did not mediate any of the causal pathways between EFs and belief reasoning. This study indicates that EFs contribute to mentalising in subtle and complex ways, and our experimental rigour reveals several methodological considerations for future research.

articles.title: Asymmetric temporal dynamics in the relationship between social media use and adolescents' wellbeing
articles.authors: Luisa Fassi; Jessica Vera Schaaf; Rogier Kievit; Laura Marciano; Amy Orben
articles.abstract: Advancing research on adolescents’ social media use and wellbeing requires methods that capture the temporal dynamics of both phenomena and their interplay. Traditional longitudinal models, even when identifying the within-person relationship between social media use and an outcome of interest, do not distinguish between effects driven by use that is greater or lesser than an individual’s average. Consequently, it remains unclear whether higher-than-usual versus lower-than-usual social media use shows similar persistence over time (autoregressive effects) and whether it has differential longitudinal relationships with wellbeing (cross-lagged effects). To address this gap, we apply an extension of the traditional random-intercept cross-lagged panel model that separately estimates autoregressive and cross-lagged effects for deviations above and below adolescents’ (N = 278, aged 14-18) within-person averages, thereby examining asymmetries. Our findings revealed asymmetric temporal dynamics that differed across social media activities and wellbeing outcomes. Autoregressive analyses showed that below-average social media use was temporally “sticky” for both active and passive use, whereas above-average use was “sticky” only for passive use. Cross-lagged analyses showed that lower-than-usual passive use predicted lower subsequent happiness and higher loneliness, while lower-than-usual use across all active and passive use predicted higher subsequent anger. Associations following above-usual use were mostly null, although above-usual video watching predicted lower happiness and higher anger; sadness showed no asymmetry. Overall, these results advance the modelling of person-specific temporal dynamics, highlighting that whether adolescents engage more or less than usual matters alongside the type of social media activity, and that wellbeing dimensions vary in their sensitivity to these temporal asymmetries.

articles.title: Welcome to the Jangle (Fallacy): The Case of Statistics and Mathematics Anxieties
articles.authors: Jenny Terry; Charlie Lea; Andy Peter Field
articles.abstract:
